prime.problem: A scheduler can always raise throughput by letting the queue grow, and averages can hide a 185 ms freeze inside a request that "passed". Without the right scoreboard you tune the wrong knob and call a failing server healthy.
prime.fits: Last card of group 1. The bottlenecks card said what limits a step; this one says how to judge the result. Every later card reports TTFT, TPOT/ITL, throughput and SLO attainment, and the policy and admission cards optimise goodput, defined here.
expect: TPOT = (E2E − TTFT) ÷ (n − 1), and ITL as each single gap
goodput and capacity under an SLO (TTFT ≤ 1 s, TPOT ≤ 50 ms)
prime.goal: Compute TTFT, TPOT, ITL and E2E from a request's token timestamps, explain why goodput, not throughput, is the scheduler's score, and spot an average that hides a stall.

attend: Request 5's TTFT is 53.5 ms, but its prefill takes only 4.8 ms. Where did the rest go, and what does that say about what TTFT measures?
How can request 442 have a 185.1 ms gap and still pass a 50 ms TPOT target?
From 20 to 60 req/s, throughput rises 1.9× while goodput falls 22%. Which queue behaviour causes both at once?
Why does a closed-loop benchmark hide queueing that an open-loop one exposes?
Why does the tighter Meta-style SLO cost only 5% of capacity here?

must: A user feels the first token and the gaps after it → TTFT = queue wait + prefill, ITL = each gap, TPOT = their mean per request → these are what an SLO is written in
TPOT averages hundreds of gaps → one 185 ms stall vanishes into a 7.9 ms mean → report percentiles and put streaming SLOs on ITL p99, not on TPOT

Past capacity, arrivals outpace completions → the queue grows without bound → throughput keeps rising (9,102 tok/s) while TTFT explodes (41% in SLO) → score the scheduler on goodput, and size fleets by capacity (40 req/s here)
elevated: Open-loop load keeps arriving whatever the server does → the queue shows up in TTFT → it is the only way to measure capacity; closed-loop load backs off and hides it
reference: the n vs n − 1 convention difference between vLLM's benchmark and Databricks
Meta's stated targets (TTFT < 350 ms, TTIT < 25 ms) and the 38 req/s result
the M3 llama-server sweep numbers (28.9 → 100.2 tok/s)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one request's timeline (arrive, queue, prefill, first token, gaps, finish) and write TTFT, ITL, TPOT and E2E on it as formulas. Then write two sentences: why averages lie, and why goodput beats throughput as the score.
checklist: TTFT = queue + prefill; E2E = TTFT + (n − 1) × TPOT
ITL is one gap; TPOT is the mean gap of one request
a single stall hides inside TPOT, so use ITL percentiles
throughput rises past capacity while goodput falls
capacity = highest rate with ≥ 99% of requests in SLO

retrieve.q: Explain why a scheduler judged on raw throughput would learn to make users wait, and what goodput adds to stop it.
answer: more requests in flight → fuller steps → more tok/s, even while the queue grows
at 60 req/s: 9,102 tok/s but 59% of users wait over 1 s
goodput counts only requests that met both SLO targets, so queueing lowers it

retrieve.q: Walk through computing request 5's TTFT, TPOT and E2E from its timestamps: arrival 4.0 ms, first token 57.5 ms, finish 91.1 ms, 8 output tokens.
Your product streams text to readers. You can put the SLO on TPOT p99 or on ITL p99. Which do you choose, and what does the other miss?
answer: ITL p99: it sees individual freezes
TPOT is a per-request mean: in E3 every request passed TPOT while 540 of 600 had a gap over 50 ms
the cost: ITL SLOs are harder to meet and push toward smaller token budgets

compare.q: Course 1 defines the same metrics for a single local model. What does a multi-user server add to their meaning, especially TTFT?
answer: on a busy server, TTFT is mostly queue: 1,397 ms p50 at 60 req/s
so a server's TTFT measures scheduling and load, not just the model

compare.q: The latency course looks at tails from the caller's side. What does this card show about where server-side tails come from, and which caller-side fix can't touch them?
answer: server tails come from queueing past capacity and from prefill stalls inside steps
a caller can hedge or retry, but a request stuck in an overloaded queue stays slow
the server-side fixes are admission control, chunked prefill and more capacity

predict.q: Two servers both report a mean TPOT of about 20 ms. Server A's gaps are all 20 ms; server B's are mostly 12 ms with a 200 ms freeze every 25 tokens. Before computing: which one does a reader notice, and which percentile would reveal it?
predict.answer: Server B: readers notice a freeze of 200 ms, while a steady 20 ms stream looks smooth. The mean hides it; ITL p99 would not, because 1 gap in 25 is 4% of gaps, well above the top 1%. A TPOT SLO of 50 ms passes both servers.

apply.task: A request arrives at t = 0 and its 5 output tokens reach the user at 120, 130, 140, 250 and 260 ms. Compute its TTFT, TPOT, E2E and worst ITL, and say whether it passes the course SLO (TTFT ≤ 1 s, TPOT ≤ 50 ms) and whether it would pass an ITL ≤ 50 ms target. Then say what on the server most likely caused the 110 ms gap.
apply.done: TTFT 120 ms, TPOT (260 − 120) ÷ 4 = 35 ms, E2E 260 ms, worst ITL 110 ms. It passes the course SLO but fails an ITL target: a long prefill joining the decode step (a generation stall) is the likely cause.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which server a reader notices, or which percentile catches it?

Which relationship is still fuzzy: queue growth → TTFT, or stall → ITL but not TPOT?
